fields.title: Vigenère Cipher
fields.theory: is a polyalphabetic substitution cipher that encrypts text by shifting each letter according to a repeating keyword.

fields.title: Mixed cipher
fields.theory: A mixed cipher is a cryptographic technique that combines both substitution and transposition methods to increase security.

fields.title: DES cipher
fields.theory: Data Encryption Standard (DES) is a symmetric block cipher that encrypts 64-bit blocks of data using a 56-bit secret key through 16 rounds of Feistel network operations

fields.title: Rail Fence Cipher
fields.theory: a form of transposition cipher that encrypts messages by writing plaintext in a zigzag pattern across a set number of "rails" (rows) and reading them off row-by-row

fields.title: Columnar Cipher
fields.theory: a symmetric transposition technique that rearranges plaintext by writing it in rows within a grid, then reading it column-by-column based on a keyword-defined order
fields.example:
Plaintext = HELLOWORLD
Keyword = ZEBRA
Ciphertext = ODLREOLLHW

fields.title: Scytale Cipher
fields.theory: ancient Greek transposition cipher (c. 7th century BC) that uses a cylinder (rod) and a spirally wrapped parchment strip to rearrange letters. The key is the rod's diameter. It encrypts by writing across the wrapped rod and decrypts by re-wrapping the strip around an identical rod.

fields.title: 3DES
fields.theory: Triple DES (3DES) is a symmetric block cipher that enhances the original DES algorithm by applying it three times to each 64-bit data block. It uses a 168-bit key (divided into three 56-bit keys) for an Encrypt-Decrypt-Encrypt (EDE) process, significantly boosting security against brute-force attacks compared to standard
fields.example:
Message: "The quick brown fox...".
Key: "1234567890123456ABCDEFGH".
Result: 13D4D3549493D2870F93C3E0812A06DE467E1F9C0BFB16C070EDE5CABBD3CA62F217A7AE8D47F2C7198FF39162ECEC94.

fields.title: AES
fields.theory: a symmetric block cipher, typically using 128-bit blocks and 128, 192, or 256-bit keys. It transforms 16-byte plaintext into 16-byte ciphertext via a 4x4 "state" matrix over 10–14 rounds (depending on key length) using Substitution-Permutation Network (SPN) principles
fields.example:
Plaintext : Two One Nine Two (16 ASCII characters, 1 byte each)
Key : Thats my Kung Fu (16 ASCII characters, 1 byte each)
Ciphertext: 29 C3 50 5F 57 14 20 F6 40 22 99 B3 1A 02 D7 3A

fields.title: Two-Fish
fields.theory: Twofish is a symmetric 128-bit block cipher developed by Bruce Schneier in 1998, featuring a 16-round Feistel network that supports keys up to 256 bits. It is highly secure, utilizing key-dependent S-boxes, a Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) matrix, and pre/post-whitening to resist cryptanalysis.
fields.example:
Plaintext: 128-bit block split into four 32-bit words.
Key: 128, 192, or 256 bits.
Result: 128-bit ciphertext.

fields.title: RSA
fields.theory: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) an asymmetric cryptographic algorithm that uses a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption, relying on the difficulty of factoring large prime numbers. It secures data through modular exponentiation, making it foundational for secure online communications (HTTPS, SSH).
fields.example:
Choose p = 3 and q = 11
Compute n = p * q = 3 * 11 = 33
Compute φ(n) = (p - 1) * (q - 1) = 2 * 10 = 20
Choose e such that 1 < e < φ(n) and e and φ (n) are coprime. Let e = 7
Compute a value for d such that (d * e) % φ(n) = 1. One solution is d = 3 [(3 * 7) % 20 = 1]
Public key is (e, n) => (7, 33)
Private key is (d, n) => (3, 33)
The encryption of m = 2 is c = 27 % 33 = 29
The decryption of c = 29 is m = 293 % 33 = 2

fields.title: Diffie-Hellman
fields.theory:
Diffie-Hellman (DH) is a cryptographic protocol allowing two parties to establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel, enabling secure, encrypted communication. It relies on the difficulty of computing discrete logarithms in finite fields. Alice and Bob exchange public values 
 derived from private, random keys  allowing both to compute the same shared secret 
 without revealing the secrets.
fields.example: important distinction: You're not sharing information during the key exchange, you're creating a key together.

fields.title: ECC
fields.theory: a modern public-key encryption technique based on the algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields. It provides high security with much smaller key sizes (e.g., 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA). Its security rests on the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP), which makes it computationally infeasible to reverse engineer a private key from a public key.
fields.example:
ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman)
ECDH is a popular key agreement protocol using ECC, where Alice and Bob generate a shared secret over an insecure channel.
